utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Registrar, if you could kindly call the case, please, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Haynes. Already standing, I see Mr. Thayer; and, of course, there's Mr. McCloskey. The witness is already present. Good morning to you, sir, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I welcome you once more. You're still testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made the first day when you started giving evidence. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Mr. President, just to give you an idea of my time estimate, I reduced examination last night, as well to accommodate one new are that was raised. There's one area I'd like to address. I think I should be able to do that in the 45 minutes that I asked for, and I would ask to be granted that indulgence based on the approximate time estimate that I made at the beginning of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear what Mr. Ostojic has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. First of all, I would like to know what the new issue is from Mr. Thayer, and just so the Court knows, we've asked the clerk, and they told us that Mr. Thayer has been one hour and 27 minutes on cross-examination, which exceeds it by close to 50 per cent, his estimate, and I don't think that it's fair and reasonable for him to go another 45 minutes. It was our understanding he was going to go 15 minutes, and based on what the Court said on Wednesday, I believe, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Ostojic, because I think this is annoying. This is annoying. I think you should know your limits as a lawyer, and you know what our prerogatives are, and you know that we use our discretion when it is necessary to use it. And when it's necessary to allow counsel to proceed, we allow counsel to proceed. But there is a limit, and let's not start the day like that. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Thayer, and try to contain it as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, we had reviewed Mr. Maric's testimony in which he recounted going to Snagovo in the early morning hours of 14 July to assist Dragan Jevtic, the Engineering Company commander. And we heard his testimony about how he linked up there with Ljubo Bojanovic and the large contingent from Doboj. Where we left off, sir, specifically was with the trial testimony of Mr. Bojanovic in the Blagojevic case, and I believe you stated that you were unaware that he testified as a Defence witness for Dragan Jokic in that case; is that correct? We may have gotten cut off mid-answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. It's true that I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me go directly to the testimony, which is 65 ter 3135, and we're at page 43 of e-court. If we scroll down to the bottom of the page, Mr. Bojanovic is asked where he spent the night of July 13th, and his answer is: "The night of 13th of July, I slept at the headquarters until 2.00 a.m., when I was awakened in order to be given certain tasks that I had to perform." And if we go to the next page, at line 19, Mr. Bojanovic testified that a messenger woke him up and told him that the chief was waiting for him in the duty operations officer room. He got dressed and went to see him. And if we turn to the next page, which is page 45 of e-court, Mr. Bojanovic testified that: "Major Obrenovic ordered me to take a part of our forces, one reinforced platoon strong plus two Pragas," Praga being an anti-aircraft two-barrel weapon, 30-millimetre in calibre, "plus one Doboj MUP platoon, and go to the area of Maricici, a village that is seven to ten kilometres away from Zvornik. He told me to leave a part of our forces there in Maricici and take a platoon of civilian police" -- sorry, "a company of civilian police commanded by Captain Zoran Jankovic, and link up the forces taken by then-Captain Maric to the area of Snagovo." Further down at line 21, he testified that: "I left from the barracks in Karakaj with the mentioned units. I passed through Zvornik. I came to the sector of Zlatne Vode, and then I took the Maricici road, where I arrived at the Maricici sector. That is where I left some of the forces, and with the rest I went towards the Snagovo sector where I was supposed to meet up with Captain Maric." And just to move things along, if we go to the next page, at line 13, the question is: "At one point you said that members of the police went with you?" And his answer was: "Yes. This was a unit that was attached for our assistance. The unit came from Doboj, and I've told you who the commander was of that unit." And the question was: "Was this the person who the next night on the 14th, in the evening, was captured by the column of the 28th Division?" Mr. Bojanovic's answer was: "Yes. When we met up with Major Maric - actually, Captain Maric - I had a different task. This was on the early morning on the 14th. I informed Captain Maric with this other captain. And afterwards I found out that after I left for this other task, that that captain was captured, the commander of the military police unit from the Doboj MUP." The next question is: "When Obrenovic issued this order to you, did he go with you or did he remain in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?" Mr. Bojanovic said: "I don't know where he was. I left with the units, so I don't know where he was after that." And the final question is: "Where did you receive this order from Obrenovic?" And the answer was: "On the 14th at 2.00 a.m. in the office of the duty operations officer." That's on the next page. And if we go to the bottom, we see that Mr. Bojanovic returned to the barracks at approximately 6.00 a.m. that same morning, the morning of the 14th. Now, sir, you no doubt heard that Doboj Platoon commander, Zoran Jankovic, was, in fact, captured by Muslim forces in the afternoon/late day of 14 July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he was captured on the 14th of July; however, I didn't learn it on that day. It was only later on that I came to know about it. I don't know whether it was on the following morning or two days later that I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall seeing Ljubo Bojanovic in that area in the early-morning hours of 14 July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see him on the 14th of July, because on that day, in the early-morning hours of that day, I was at Maricici and he was at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to Mr. Maric's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can have 65 ter 3138 on the screen, please, and that's page 62 of e-court. Actually, if we could go back four pages to page 11599, please. My apologies. That's page 58 of e-court. I just wanted to pick up one point. And if we could actually go to the next page, 11600, page 59, at line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, sir, testified that in the morning of 14 July, and this is at line 16: "When I was touring the men, I had deployed at certain positions. I saw those two prisoners, and that was when the chief of staff arrived, around 8.00 or 9.00. I was present when these prisoners were questioned." And the next question is: "And who questioned these prisoners?" And Mr. Maric replied: "The chief of staff personally." And at the bottom of the page, he says: "I was there while the prisoners were being questioned."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go again to page 11602, page 62 of e-court -- 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At line 4, Mr. Maric testified that: "In that period, while the prisoners of war were being questioned, Zoran Jovanovic came, the operations officer from the brigade, and he brought a group of 50 to 60 soldiers as reinforcement. Then, in that period, I noticed two prisoners who had surrendered to the military police. They were boarded onto a truck. I also saw a couple of soldiers boarding the truck. I think that these were two soldiers from the engineers, from Dragan Jevtic's unit, about three or four donors. And I could see a small number of people leaving. I asked Jevtic, 'Where are you going? Where are these people going?' And he said, 'Under Obrenovic's orders, we're leaving.' Obrenovic was there. He was about ten metres away from where this was happening." Now, you already told us, sir, that you do recall seeing Mr. Maric while you were at Snagovo. Do you recall seeing Mr. Jevtic while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that because I never did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say, sir, then, that you never saw two members of the Engineering Company being sent back from that area any time on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see them, because on the 14th of July I had only just come back to the barracks from Maricici; and between 11.00 and 12.00, I set out again for Maricici and took along a group of soldiers from Maricici to Snagovo. I wasn't able to see them at all, because if they went there, they probably used a vehicle. I was not able to see these members of the engineering unit or Maric at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page, 11603, and that's page 62 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page, the question is: "And what happened then on the 14th in the evening, in the afternoon?" And the answer was: "After we finished with the prisoners, the chief ordered the unit to organise itself and to start to search the terrain ahead in order to go towards the column that was coming in. Up until about 1800 hours, the deployment proceeded. Zoran's men, the military police, they were being deployed, and they began to search the terrain." Now, let me just ask you, sir: Having heard that portion of the testimony, who do you think the "Zoran" is to whom Mr. Maric was referring?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to be told, I don't know which "Zoran" is referred to by Maric here. I only know that on the 14th, I set out to scour the terrain at around 1400 hours and I ended at 1700 hours, whereupon I pulled up towards Snagovo, where I saw the chief of staff, Obrenovic, and his driver. In the evening hours, I can tell you for a fact that no terrain was being searched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry. I think if the complete answer is written, maybe it would help the witness, because on the next page, the reference is also page 11604, a certain "Zoran," and that's just a completion the answer that Mr. Thayer read. I think, in fairness to the witness, it may assist him in which Zoran this Maric was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ostojic is right, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, Mr. Maric testified that: "At around 1800 or 1830 hours, we clashed with the column of Muslims. It was quite an intense clash. The fighting didn't last very long, perhaps for about half an hour or so or an hour. Then there was sporadic fire afterwards. Many of our fighters were killed at that time. There were ones that were captured as well, and you could hear on the radio that the commander, Major Zoran, from the command was captured. He was the one who had brought the civilian police, the special police from Doboj, and they were asking for a halt of the fire. The fire was halted later. We continued to pull out our forces which had dispersed in contact with the enemy, and this pullout went on until quite late into the night, until about 2300 hours." Now, sir, you were in this general area during this time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was up there at the time, but I was again at Snagovo roughly from 1400 hours, when the searches of the terrain started and when we came to the foot of Velja Glava, and this ended at 1700 hours. As we started descending towards Velja Glava, we stopped there because we could hear shooting from the area of Liplje and Maricici. Beyond us, a column of Muslim forces was passing. We did not engage in combat of any sort. We didn't exchange fire. I was with the soldiers who were under the commander of Zoran, but he wasn't a major, he was a platoon commander. When this ended, when the column went past us, we decided to pull out toward the old school building up at Snagovo. As we reached Snagovo, I saw Obrenovic there, and I spent the night up there at Snagovo. During my stay at Snagovo, during the night that I spent at Snagovo, we did not engage the enemy in combat of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Well, this is precisely why I asked you the question in the way that I did, because now it seems that you're telling us that you, in fact, had police troops under your command on the 14th of July. If I'm reading the transcript, you just said that: "I was with the soldiers who were under the command of Zoran." I think you've been consistent in telling us that on the 14th, when you returned to that area, you were only in the presence and leading soldiers from the Zvornik Brigade. Which is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I say? I said that I was leading the soldiers from the Zvornik Brigade. The "Zoran" that I'm mentioning was a member of the Zvornik Brigade who had a platoon under his command. The extent of my contacts with the civilian police was only to take them up at Maricici. The they were not under my command. They were independently performing their assignment. I was merely introducing -- my role was merely to take them to take up their positions and to return on the 14th, nothing more than that. They were not members of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I took the police forces up there, I returned; and then on the 14th I went up to Snagovo with the army to link up the line from Maricici to Snagovo, to fill out the gaps that weren't manned by a single soldier. I did as much, and I started the searching of the terrain at roughly 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I just want to clarify one thing, based on your answer. Your response to me a few moments ago, that this Zoran was not a major, that he was a platoon commander, was in response to you hearing the testimony from Mr. Maric that you could hear on the radio that the commander, Major Zoran, was captured. He was the one who had brought the civilian police, the special police from Doboj. And you just went out of your way to correct me to say that: "No, no. That Major Zoran was actually a platoon commander."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I said that Major Zoran Jovanovic, which is me, brought the civilian police at Maricici. I said that I met up with the platoon commander beyond Velja Glava. He was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. His name was Zoran. I don't know what his family name was. I didn't say that he was Zoran Jovanovic. Zoran Jovanovic brought the police on the 14th at Maricici. The this is something that I was stating all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the only Zoran that was captured on the 14th was the Doboj Platoon commander, correct, Zoran Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the commander from Doboj, nor can I be able to say that I received a report on the radio about his capture or his name. What I said was that I heard only later that the commander of the civilian police unit had been captured. What his name was, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 11659, which is should be 118 in e-court, but I think my math is off this morning, so it might be 119. It is 118. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at line 9, the question was put to Mr. Maric: "Do you recall telling the investigators when you interviewed in Banja Luka that you had heard Obrenovic on the radio during the day on the 14th of July?" And the answer is: "Yes. He was in command when the operations began. He was with us until we began to spread out. Then I went to the right flank. I didn't physically see him. But later when the combat operations started, when we clashed with the enemy, I heard him over the radio, over the radio connection. And then when I actually came to the Snagovo road, he was already there." The question is: "What time was this when you saw him on the Snagovo road on the 14th, roughly?" Answer: "The pullout lasted until about 22 or 2300 hours. He was up there. We waited until all of the soldiers pulled out, so that we could see what the situation was in terms of the numbers." Then the next question is: "Okay. Let me see if this refreshes your recollection. Well, of course, you've already testified on the morning of the 14th, you saw him in the Snagovo area. In fact, he interrogated some of those prisoners; correct?" And Mr. Maric answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is on the next page at the top, 119 in e-court:

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "I know that he questioned them. He interrogated them. After that was finished, he waited for Zoran to come, and then he ordered what he ordered." Now, sir, I put it to you that the "Zoran" that Mr. Maric is referring to here is you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are claiming. However, if he had been waiting for Zoran Jovanovic, then Zoran Jovanovic could only have come after 12.00 to the area where I was headed to conduct the scouring of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we just go down quickly to the bottom of this page, Mr. Maric testifies that with respect to Major Obrenovic: " ... I know that immediately prior to the clash with the Muslim forces, I could hear him over the radio. He commanded throughout the entire operation during the pullout, and then when the truce went into force. So he was constantly on the radio. Once I got to the road, physically reached the road, I saw him there. He was in a vehicle. By that time, it was already dark. When the pullout was completed, it was already dark, so it was probably quite late." And, sir, how does this comport with your recollection of seeing Mr. Obrenovic later in the day of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I saw Obrenovic only at around 1800 hours, or, rather, between 1700 hours and 1900 hours. I cannot tell you the precise time but it was towards the evening, because we were pulling out from below Velja Glava to Snagovo. I don't know how long the pullout had lasted, but I only know that once we reached the old school, we were tasked to billet there and to head for the new school, where we spent the night. Only on the morning of the 15th, I was ordered to go back. I cannot tell you about the other forces. I know that my part of the unit withdrew towards the evening to Snagovo, let's say, around 1800 or 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there is evidence in this case from one of those two Engineering Company members who was sent to Snagovo and then ordered to return to the base, and he testified in the Blagojevic case that he went up there the night of the 13th, going into the 14th, and that he saw Major Obrenovic at Snagovo at about 4.00 a.m. in the morning of 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's in the testimony of Milos Mitrovic, for the record, which is 65 ter number 2259 admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where do you recall being at 4.00 a.m. on the morning of 14 July, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was in Maricici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give me the 65 ter number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. That's 2259, and the transcript references for that exhibit are 5597 to 5599. Now, if we could have 65 ter 3465, and if we go to page 34. I think that's of both the document and of e-court, and if we could go to the bottom of the page, please. It's going to be the next page. I think the pagination changed when we put it into e-court. That's it. If we could go to the bottom of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at page 19, and this is an OTP -- that is an interview conducted by investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor with Mr. Dragan Jevtic on 13 December 1999, and Mr. Jevtic says: "Now it's the 14th. On 14, in the morning, I don't remember exactly what time was it, one person, one young man arrested was brought there. I remember he was very young, and that he sat there and ate one kilo of bread right away without anything, just bread. Major Obrenovic was with him, and they started questioning. One of the questions was how many people are with them, and then I heard that he said there were 20 or 30 coming behind him. That young man was taken later on for further questioning in the brigade command." And this is page 29 in the B/C/S: "We stayed there until 2.00 in the afternoon. Then Major Obrenovic told us, to our line and the rest of the soldiers, that we cannot wait for them, that we have to go first, so the movement started. I was at the end."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's also the next page, and we're there at page 3422, end of the ERN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we have another person who recalls seeing Major Obrenovic interrogating a prisoner in the morning of 14 July. And if we could go back to page 23, I just want to pick up one thing before we move on, and it will have to be the next page because of this pagination issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtic is asked the question: "Do you remember the code name which was used by Maric for the purpose, the radio code name?" And his answer was: "Yes, I do remember it, Jasen." Do you recall that code name being used during that period of time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the code names used during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These radio names were used on a daily basis and they were changed regularly, so it is difficult for me to tell you and to name these code names to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 2231, and the English version is at 2232.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm going to show you are some excerpts from a notebook maintained by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which recorded tactical intercepts; that is, intercepted radio communications between various VRS forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have page 9 of the B/C/S first, and we'll have to see how legible this is on e-court. We'll have to go up to ERN ending in 8949, please, and if we could go down a little bit. Right there is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you read that? Is that okay or do you need the original?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at it. There is mention here of Ljubo, Jasen, Sidro, which are meaningless to me, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you can take my word for it, sir, that this entry in this book is the list of the -- refers to the list of the active frequencies and users on 13 July 1995, Thursday. That section you just referred to follows a section where the intercept operators are noticing that there's all of a sudden a lot of activity towards the end of the night and early-morning hours of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think we have got the wrong English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The English should be page 4, Mr. President, at the top. My apologies. May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're just trying to match the B/C/S with the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's not easy with the way it's formatted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We were just wondering if the witness was able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He went, actually, Your Honour, to the section I was going to by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So where we are is there's an entry that reflects a lot of activity on the radio net in the early-morning hours of the 14th of July; late night 13, early-morning hours of the 14th. The line you just looked at reads: "They informed Lovac." That's the com centre, is that right, or that doesn't ring a bell for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's okay. I'll move on, sir: "They informed Lovac about all movements of our troops, Premier, Strsljen," and in parentheses, it says "Ljubo." Do you have any knowledge of Mr. Bojanovic using that code ever, "Strsljen"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly don't know anything about this. Each unit was given its own code name. And if we were to meet, for example, Ljubo and I, I would also have his code name. However, I cannot tell you exactly who was using which code name. If it says here that Lovac was to be informed, this probably refers to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, then we see there's a reference to Jasen, and we just that was Mr. Maric's code. The final line is: "Those were attached units that arrived during the night." Now, if we could go, and this is the last page on the document I want to refer your attention to, to page 6 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go down to the bottom of the page. Bear with me, please, one moment. I'm sorry. We're going to need to go back one page. And if we can scroll down, and then pop over to the next page, please, we'll be looking at the middle of the page on the next page. There's an entry for -- okay. If we could just scroll up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the entry that says "Lovac, Lovac 1" towards the top of the page in B/C/S, and this is the top of the page of page 6 in English. This is from the 14th of July, in the afternoon: "Lovac, Lovac 1. Check in the base of Zoran Jankovic --" sorry, "Zoran Jovanovic has set off already, and then let me know. He's leaving just now. Have him hurry up." This suggests that you were still on the move and that Major Obrenovic was still waiting for you to arrive on the afternoon of the 14th of July. How does that comport with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at Snagovo on the 14th of July, after 12.00, so that was actually early afternoon, and we started to scour the terrain at 1400 hours. Those were our orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you P383. On this day, the 14th of July, sir, it's fair to say that the Zvornik Brigade had mobilised virtually every able-bodied person it could in the brigade to be in the field, to protect the town of Zvornik and the settlements along the route that the VRS expected the retreating column of Muslim soldiers and military-aged men to be following; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade command that mobilised the men, and this is something that the commander and the drafting office know. No other person should know about that; only people who are entrusted with forming the units were subsequently informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, my question is a little bit more simple than that. There was an extraordinarily grave threat to the municipality of Zvornik during this period of time, was there not, and that's why all of these units and mixed forces, police and reservists, were being mobilised; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a serious threat, and the commanders and the command of police and everybody else knew about that. However, we, who were operations personnel in units, we were not supposed to or we shouldn't have known that. I do know that there was a great danger. Why men were mobilised, it was done because it had been established that there was a large number of Muslim men who managed to pull out of Srebrenica and whose intention was to cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 8, I hope, in e-court, and this is page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, sir, is a page from the barracks duty officer notebook. Are you familiar with the notebook that was maintained in connection with the situation in the barracks on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Records were kept in the office of the operations duty officer of all reports received from the positions, and this is called the duty operations officer's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I'm referring to is a different book that was referred to as the barracks duty officer book, in which someone was tasked each day to record the comings and goings of visitors and the general state of the barracks. Do you recall such a notebook being maintained at Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never had this hand [as interpreted] in my book -- in my hands, because it was up to other organs to keep this kind of records.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we look at the bottom of the page, sir, do you see the reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, that's page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom of page 6 of the English, it says: "A body of troops at the barracks was not counted due to the activities in the field, and practically only operations duty officer and guards were at the barracks." Now, sir, the Trial Chamber's heard a lot of evidence that on the 14th of July, that the barracks were virtually empty because everybody was being sent to the terrain. In fact, we've heard that they even sent the lawyers to the terrain. So you know they were in trouble if they're sending lawyers to the terrain. Now, would you not expect Major Obrenovic, as a good commander, to be in the field during that day on the 14th of July, as the man in charge of the brigade, because that's where he should be, where the main effort, the main threat was concentrated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw Dragan Obrenovic, that was in Snagovo between 1700 hours and 1900 hours; and on that occasion, I received an order from him at the barracks, on the 14th, to lead the army and to link them up with our police in order to conduct the search of the terrain. Then I saw him on the evening of the 14th in Snagovo. Since he had a car, he was mobile. He could -- he was able to come up there and go down. I was not in his escort, and I cannot tell you exactly what his movements were. I just told you when and where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just heard that Mr. Maric and Mr. Bojanovic testified about linking up with each other in Maricici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, if you could kindly wind up and finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We'll be calling on you to finish within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the testimony of Mr. Maric and Mr. Bojanovic about linking up with each other in Maricici in the early-morning hours between the 13th and 14th of July, but neither of those gentlemen mentions seeing you there with the Doboj police at that time. Do you have an explanation for that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This is my explanation: The night between the 13th and the 14th, I spent at Maricici. The units of Maric and Ljubo Bojanovic, who they took up there, were not even close to Maricici, because Snagovo is quite a way from Maricici. The two are linked only with a trail, practically, that could be trafficable only by foot and not through -- by vehicles. I did not see either Maric or Bojanovic close to Maricici at all. It is for them to state whatever they wish to. I can tell you that they were not at Maricici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could quickly go to P0377.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday a 19 July daily combat report that referred to members of the 16th Krajina Brigade being present in the zone of responsibility of Commander Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade, and about two soldiers who were captured on 13 and eliminated or liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at page 160, and it's also the English page 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You'll see a reference to IKM, that is, forward command post, Ljubo reported that men from the 16th Krajina are at trig point 6002 - that's at the very bottom of the page, sir - and that Obrenovic should be informed. Now, you testified yesterday about what was characterized to you as the prevailing practice at the time concerning the treatment of prisoners, and you made a point of saying that it wouldn't make sense if they captured two and executed the rest, because they would have executed everybody if that's what they had wanted to do. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That referred to the two that were captured and 13 who were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, we may have a translation issue here, to be fair to the witness and the record, Mr. President. The witness said "13 executed." I just want to ask whether that's what he said or what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, sir? The transcript refers to you answer, saying: "That referred to the two that were captured and 13 who were executed." My question to you, because I want to make sure we get what you say correctly is: Did you say the 13 that were executed or did you say something else, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the daily combat report referred to two captured and 13 liquidated. No, I didn't say ever that they were executed. "Liquidated" meant that in the course of combat, they were liquidated, or that's to say 13. Two of them probably surrendered themselves, and that's why it was said that they were taken prisoner. No, I didn't say that they were executed. That meant that you actually captured them and then you shot them. "Liquidated" means in the course of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony from a witness who survived an execution near Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is PW-139.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He describes there being with a group of about 20 people who came under fire, and then watching several of the people he was with being executed in front of him until he was kept alive, he said, because the Serb soldiers thought he had value as a soldier for exchange. Now, I want to show you very quickly 65 ter 3459?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's page 10 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, last paragraph, and if we could just go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, but this exhibit is not on the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's on the list that we distributed this morning, and I distributed hard copies to everybody before the decision and specifically advised people of the topic that I would be addressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But please conclude in the next two minutes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can scroll down, please, there is a reference to, "at the site of the village of Krizevici," a location called "Brezjak." There's some coordinates that are given. Do you see those coordinates, sir, CQ 41.7-22.6?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put it to you, and just to save time, I won't show you the maps we've got, but just north of trig point 602, which was reported as the location of the 16th Krajina Brigade on the 18th, just north of that location, at those coordinates, a mass grave was exhumed, and the remains of one of the people who PW-139 testified seeing executed were recovered from that mass grave, sir. Now, you testified yesterday about that daily combat report and what you understood happened that day. Having heard this information, that there's been a DNA match putting one of the people that PW-139 said was with him and executed at this location at Nezuk on the 19th of July, the day you wrote that daily combat report, does that change your conclusion about what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I'm wrong. Could the Prosecutor tell us the identity of the people who were found in this mass grave, or at least a group identity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can do that in private session. It's in evidence, and I can give the name of the one person that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session straight away, then, and do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified about what that daily combat report meant, and I'm asking you: Having heard this information, does that change your understanding of what happened that day and the treatment of prisoners that day, or is it still your position that Muslim prisoners were treated correctly on all occasions that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first answer in relation to the daily combat report. A daily combat report is written on the basis of the reports received from the battalion commands, i.e., the subordinate units which were duty-bound on reporting the events and activities of the date. This daily combat report refers to two persons captured and 13 killed. I stand by what I said, that these wounds and deaths were the result of combat. As far as the treatment of prisoners is concerned, I can tell you what my conduct was in that respect and what I believe was the conduct of the brigade command. I can't tell what it is, the treatment. I only can tell you that I know of the four prisoners that I sent on to the brigade command. It was not my duty to deal with that segment, the treatment and the dealings with the prisoners of war. I do believe, however, that this was the treatment accorded to them, the proper treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you have a re-examination. I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarapa, do you have a re-examination, too? I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Jovanovic, again.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us first clarify certain details that remained unclear with relation to the Doboj police unit. I will therefore show certain documents to you and ask you to look at them. Let us start with the exhibit shown to you by the Prosecutor, which is document 3138. He showed you pages 60 and 62, and I will show you page 61. I want to take you to the earlier page, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the page before this one, page 60. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at lines 9 and 10. Among other things, he says there: [In English] "There was a major there as well. I think his name was Zoran, who had brought a special unit from Doboj." [Interpretation] This is my first question: Did you hold the rank of major at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there someone else in your unit whose name was Zoran and who had the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at another Prosecution exhibit, from their list; namely 3430. I don't know if the document has been translated, but I will refer to it only briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you conclude that this is an official note of interview -- official record of an interview, that the date is the 16th of August, 1995, and that it was drafted by the State Security Service in Tuzla? Do you see that much?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the heading up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph states the source, where you have the name of Zoran Jankovic, his personal background, and the second line says: "Active policeman of the Public Security Centre in Doboj, the Traffic Safety Station in Modrici." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see next, as part of his personal background, the mention of any sort of rank?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to page 3 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the paragraph that was marked by someone earlier on, which says, as part of the CJB Doboj, there is the police -- special purpose police detachment, numbering around 150 men. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although the legibility is quite poor, but I can see the mention of 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now turn to page 13 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph starts at follows, "On the 13th of July, 1995 ... "

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read it out to you: "On the 13th of July, 1995, pursuant to a decision by the chief of the Public Security Station in Doboj, from Jankovic's police station for traffic safety, the following persons were sent out to the Zvornik battlefield." Next follow various names which I will skip, except for the last name, which is that "Zoran Jankovic." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The paragraph below, the first sentence of the paragraph that follows, states the total of 97 men were deployed to the Zvornik battlefield from the Doboj CJB. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And we can see that they are from the stations from Doboj, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, Teslic, and Odzak. The next sentence reads: "The commander of this company was Dragan Gavric." Let me find the relevant part. Please bear with me until I find the right passage. The following paragraph talks about what this group that was deployed did on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And there the platoon commanders who made up the group are mentioned. Do you see there, in line 3, that the commander of the 3rd Platoon was Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at document 4D394.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order which came from the office of the Ministry of Interior, dated the 13th of July, 1995, sent to several addresses in Doboj. We have the abbreviation "CBP," "SOP Doboj." I don't know if you know what these abbreviations stand for. But since the order is quite short - I don't know if it has been translated or not, I believe it has - it reads: "Form forthwith a reinforced police unit which will be composed of the 1st Company of the PJP Doboj and elements of the forces of the SOP Doboj." The next sentence reads: "The unit is duty-bound to report to Zvornik during the course of the day, where it will be given specific assignments. Upon the deployment of the unit, a report to that effect should be sent with reference to the above number." It's signed by Deputy Minister of the Interior. I believe the name is Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just see the signature on the bottom of the page, please. Can we now look at another document, which is 4D399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wondering, because you didn't actually ask a question, whether you are combining this document with the next one and then put the question. I don't know what your intention is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put a question to you right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see, on the basis of this, from the order of the Ministry of the Interior, that the unit should report on the 13th of July, on the same day when that order was issued in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this physically possible at all, for the unit to reach Zvornik from Doboj by the time you set out for Maricici with a part of the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's physically possible because the distance between Doboj and Zvornik is 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at the document you have on your screen, which reads -- or, rather, this is the response from the 5th Police Detachment, as the document says, and the document has a date of the 13th of July, 1995, which reads: "Elements of the forces of the 5th Detachment of the SBP Doboj was deployed to its destination at 1200 hours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The detachment commander signed it. What I'd like to know is whether, on the basis of this, you are able to infer, on the basis of what you know, that this unit did not arrive as a whole to Zvornik. First one part of this group reached Zvornik, followed by the second?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in how many groups they arrived. Let me just correct what I've said about the distance. It's a bit over 100 kilometres because you went across Bijeljina and Brcko to reach Zvornik, but it was physically possible to reach Zvornik quite swiftly. I don't know if the group arrived as a whole or in several batches. I only know that ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the hour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: ... that at that time, this group that I sent over to Maricici arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also, Mr. Zivanovic, if you could clarify this. In the English page of the document, it says that part of the forces were sent to the destination, but your question was interpreted as they were deployed. So I'm not aware of the nuances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quoting the text, which says part of the forces of the 5th Detachment of the SBJ Doboj was sent to its destination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: This was the translation from the original by the interpreter in the booth, since we don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it was interpreted differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But on the basis of this, would you conclude that they set out from Doboj at about 1200 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this letter, it says that they were sent at 1200 hours, which means that they -- that was the time when they left Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Time for a break, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more do you require, how much more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe not less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Sarapa, how much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Five minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, at the beginning, I wanted to present to you all these segments of Maric's testimony, but my learned colleague beat me to it. He showed all this to you, and I'm not going to repeat myself. I think that the replies that you have given are quite sufficient in order to interpret this Maric's testimony in a true light. Let me ask you something different. I am referring to the code names that were used on the ground, and I'm specifically referring to tactical intercept. When you went to the terrain, or any other high-ranking officers from the brigade, for that matter, were they accompanied by any person who was taking care that they have communications with the Command and with other parts of the brigade that were on location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A communications officer would accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 13th, and on the 14th, 15th and 16th, as you described, did you have a communications officer with you as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the night of the 13th; but on the 13th and 15th and 16th, I had a communications officer with me in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please -- let us just repeat the dates. You said, on one of the dates, he wasn't there, and tell us on which dates he was there. Can you repeat that, please, just to correct the transcript, because there was a slight mistake.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, when I went on Maricici to search the terrain, and then again on the 15th and 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you set off on the 14th to Maricici, and there was another place you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the day when you didn't have a communications officer, what date was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the night of the 13th, when I took the police to Maricici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you want to establish communication with the Command or other parts of your units, are you doing that personally or is that being done by a communications officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A communications officer establishes the line. If I need to speak to the Command, then it is I who speak to them. If, however, some information has to be passed on, then I tell the communications officer to do it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the communications officer has to be familiar with all the code names applicable to the Command and everybody else that you are communicating with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a plan of communications containing all the code names of commands and staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, was it your duty to know which particular code was used by any unit on a particular day, or was it his duty to know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was up to the communications officer to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So it was not your obligation to be familiar with these secret codes assigned to certain parts of units or individual officers on a particular day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to know them, but I didn't have to have a list of the names with me. That was something that the communications officer had to have with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, for example, if you asked the communications officer to connect you to, let's say, Ljubo Bojanovic or somebody else, are you going to say, "Connect me to Ljubo Bojanovic," or do you have to say, "Connect me with Pauk, Snail, Wasp," or any other code name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I order a communications officer to establish a connection, I can only do so with the persons with whom I have the plan of work, and that is the plan of work for that particular day, and I can only communicate with the persons contained in this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question was: How did you tell him the name of the commander? Would you give him full name or would you give him the code name of the person you wished to call?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to say the code name. Suffice it to say, "Call the commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the Prosecution Exhibit 3435 that the Prosecutor has shown to you. It contained a conversation or an intelligence report -- correction. It's a report on the interview with Dragan Obrenovic, and I would like to ask you a few questions in this respect. You, according to your recollection, you testified here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to keep the record clear, Your Honour, this does not reflect the conversation with Dragan Obrenovic, but with an attorney representing Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. It might have been my mistake. This was a conversation with the lawyer of Dragan Obrenovic, not Dragan Obrenovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection, you said that present during this interview was an American lawyer, an interpreter, and Obrenovic's brother, and someone else whom you cannot remember. I would like to ask you: Do you remember where you met these people? What kind of building was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in an office near the monument in Zvornik. As far as I can remember, that used to be a law firm office. I'm not sure. But it is right next to the monument in the center of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who asked you questions? Was it our colleague from the United States, through the interpreter, or did someone else ask you questions? Did you have any direct communication without an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the questions were posed by the American lawyer, and we communicated through the interpreter because my knowledge of English -- of the English language is not sufficient for us to communicate directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if anyone wrote down your answers or anything that transpired during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably noted it down, but to tell you the truth, I didn't pay attention to that. Probably, a record has to be kept if you're asking someone questions and getting answers from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if they offered you to have this conversation audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if they proposed to compile a written statement that you could possibly sign?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, had they made such a proposal, I would have signed this statement. I have no reason to hide anything, and I also have no reason not to sign what I say orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this statement, or at least in this conversation as presented to us - you only have an English version in front of you, and I translated it when we did the briefing, and this was also put to you by the Prosecutor - I see that it says that you could not remember who had given you the order to go to Maricici, to Snagovo, et cetera. What I would like to hear is the following: During the conversation, did the lawyer who questioned you ask you who was the person who was competent to send you there? I suppose that would be a useful piece of information for him, because it concerns his client.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, I don't remember being asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know for what reasons were they interested in your movements, where you went in those days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were interested in my movements, on whose orders, that was probably the motive for their interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, you said that you remember these dates and events by taking the Baljkovica battle and the opening of the corridor as reference points. I remember you saying that. In this conversation, as interpreted in this document, there is a description of what you were doing over the course of four days, but we do not have the dates for these days. So let us go through these four days, and let us try to reconstruct the dates from the statement that you gave in 2001 -- excuse me, not the statement; rather, the conversation that you had with the Defence counsel of Dragan Obrenovic. I'm going to begin with the first five passages of this report. It contains some general information which I'm not going to ask you about, but let us focus on paragraph 6. I'm going to read it out to you, because you cannot understand it otherwise: [In English] " One night," he doesn't remember the exact date, "at about 2130 p.m., someone asked him," he doesn't know who, "whether he was willing to go with the civilian police unit to Maricici. He spent the night there. In the morning, the next day somebody," he doesn't know who, "from Standard called him to return back to Standard." [Interpretation] Based on this event, can you tell me what particular day this refers to, of all the days that you mention the throughout your testimony? In other words, the day when you went to Maricici, what was the date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 13th, and the morning was on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we see a description, an account of your activities on the 14th. That's the remaining part of this page, and it reads as follows: [In English] "Someone said," he doesn't know by whom, "to get about 60 to 70 men with him and go to Snagovo." [Interpretation] I am not going to read all this in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now just move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that you reached Snagovo at [In English] "... 14 hours, and it was then that he first saw Dragan Obrenovic for the first time." [Interpretation] Therefore, I'm not going to go into details, but can you tell me, about this particular day, which day is that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 4 on this page: [In English] "The next day, in the morning, Jovanovic went to Orahovac. There was visible traces on the grass showing that the Muslim column had passed along Perunika." [Interpretation] There is no need for me to continue reading. You told us what you did in Orahovac. Can you tell us which date this was in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are now going to skip the next three paragraphs and move on to paragraph 8, which reads: [In English} "There was heavy combat in Baljkovica. Near Krizevici, they captured four Muslim men. One of them had a hunting rifle. These men were interrogated; and after half an hour, at the most, they were sent by TAM truck to the Zvornik Brigade under the escort of four soldiers." [Interpretation] And now -- I apologise. One part of my quotation is missing, and I'm going to read it again: [In English] " ... combat in Baljkovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I repeat the whole paragraph again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is paragraph 8: [In English] "The next day there was heavy combat in Baljkovica. Near Krizevici, they captured four Muslim men. One of them had a hunting rifle. These men were interrogated; and after half hour at the most they were sent by TAM truck to the Zvornik Brigade under the escort of four soldiers." [Interpretation] So now you mentioned the names of two soldiers, and you say the following in the next paragraph: "That day Mrga, [Previous translation continues ...] [In English] "... Baljkovica. Jovanovic heard that Vinko ordered the opening of the corridor. The same day he returned to the office in Standard."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're missing again the beginning of the quotation; namely, words: "That day Mrga, [In English] one of the Drina Wolves was killed in Baljkovica. Jovanovic heard that Vinko ordered the opening of the corridor. The same day he returned to the office in Standard."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me what date was this, in relation to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So, when we reconstruct this conversation that you -- that the representatives of Dragan Obrenovic had with you, can you see any difference between what was said in this report and what you described to us here? I'm focusing only on the dates. I'm not talking about Obrenovic or other things.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there are no discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Neither can I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 377, page 160. Can we look at the bottom of the page, and can it be enlarged so that the witness can see it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the last entry on the bottom of the page says: "Ljubo has informed that from the 16th Krajina are at TT 602, and Obrenovic shall be informed about this." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: What does "TT" stand for, this abbreviation, "TT 602"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means "trig point."

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You mean trig point, you would agree with mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this will be corrected at line 18, page 41, it's not a "cross-examination" by Mr. Sarapa, but it's a "re-examination" by Mr. Sarapa. So please proceed, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Does TT point 602, mentioned here, actually indicate Cetino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You are familiar with the terrain. How far is Cetino Brdo from Krizevici, if you know where Cetino Brdo is, and I presume you do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know approximately where Cetino Brdo is; but as for the distance, I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Where are Motovo and Motovska Kosa?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of these places, but I don't know exactly where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the document that was used by the Prosecution during the examination, and the number is P3459, page 5 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. Can we please see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please look at the last paragraph, which begins on the location, and can you read it through the first three lines. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this is a text which says: "On the locality of the village of Krizevici, hamlet of Zulici, the site called Brezjak, the site where sand is extracted, the location called Kum, owned by Safeta Smajlovic of Motovo, a mass grave was found containing the remains of eight individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, could you please repeat your question? The interpreters note that they had a delay because they had to interpret from the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what does that mean? Can we proceed? I suggest you repeat your question, please, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: This is the question: Is the witness aware of and has the witness heard of Muslims who were killed in Baljkovica having been buried at Motovska Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't heard him giving any answer. Mr. Jovanovic, you're still reading or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting to be told to confirm my answer. I answered that I was not aware of that. That was before your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Let me put another question to you. Is Motovo close to Krizevici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you if it's close to Krizevici. I know the location of Krizevici, but I can't tell you where exactly Motovo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. Jovanovic, we don't have any further questions for you, which means that you can go. Your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony; and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the documents. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are asking to tender five documents used in re-examination of the witness. This is Prosecution document 3138, 3430, and 3435, and 4D394 and 4D399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None. They are so admitted. Mr. Sarapa, do you have any?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. There is -- there is no written in the transcript: "4D392 and 4D399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, do you have an indication of these documents? Do you have the details of these documents? Yes. Okay. Mr. Sarapa, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the documents I've used have already been admitted: 3D377, 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat them if you are not tendering them. Mr. Thayer, do you have any documents that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President. We have 65 ter number 3112 - and this is a list that's been distributed - 65 ter 3429, 65 ter 3434, 65 ter 3435, 65 ter 3442, 65 ter 3459, and 65 ter 3465. Just based on the redirect examination of Mr. Sarapa, I would also just offer from the bar table a simple NATO map that I had intended to show the witness, but cut out to save time. It's not marked in any fashion. It's up-loaded in e-court. My friends were informed I was going to use it. It's 3463, and it has the coordinates on it that will track to the exhumation report and, I think, will assist the Court with particularly some of the questions that my learned friend Mr. Sarapa just had for the witness. I would just offer that from the bar table as a simple map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone? No objection. So that is admitted as well, and it will be given a number by our registrar. All right. I think we can move to the next witness. In the meantime, for the record, I notice the presence of Ms. Lada Soljan and Mr. Rupert Elderkin in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we start, there is, in relation to this witness, a motion from the Popovic Defence team, before the addition of certain exhibits, the Rule 65 ter exhibits list, exhibits which relate to the report of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have the witness not here, Mr. President? I have a preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you accompany him back out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt you, Mr. President, because it had to do with the subject you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that you had a preliminary; otherwise, I would have asked you to intervene straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's actually right on the subject you're discussing right now. I don't know if you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Obviously, I mean, I'm raising the motion of the Popovic Defence team precisely because it needs to be decided before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the position on that is I object, in part, to this motion. I object to the expert report, specifically, and let me explain why. This witness, it's my understanding - and I would have preferred to file our objections on this because it's an important topic regarding potential military expertise - however, I have been discussing this witness and this matter with Mr. Zivanovic for a long time now to try to get to the bottom of what this witness was going to be testifying about. And it's only in the last couple of days that we have gotten really some idea of what this is about. We received his expert report on Wednesday, and only in Serbian. We still don't have it in English. Then we've got this filing of yesterday with all these exhibits, but I can briefly outline our position. It was my understanding this witness was principally called in order to counter a definition that CLSS gave of the term "rukovodjenje." They translated "rukovodjenje" as "control." Mr. Jovanovic had said he felt that "management" was the proper terminology. And it was my understanding that this witness was fluent in English and was going to explain their view on why they thought "management" was the appropriate term instead than "control." You may recall me saying: "Whether it be management or control, the Prosecution is not suggesting either is a command function on the part of a security officer." So it wasn't that kind of an issue. So then we received the 65 ter summary, and it starts off with: "If assignment granted, the expert will explain the main difference between the four B/C/S military concepts "rukovodjenje," komandovanje, rukovodjenje u strucnom." Thank you. In any event, we can see that as its written down. Then it says, "... from the report of Petar Vuga." Now, this caused me alarm because all these concepts are discussed by Petar Vuga in his report, Petar Vuga being an expert in security affairs. So I don't -- I did not understand why we were getting someone else to talk about someone else's report that also fully defines it. So then I asked Mr. Zivanovic about that, and he said that he would or he may be discussing -- this witness may be discussing this to put it in context to help with the issue related to translation. So I said, "Okay. As long as it's limited to translation and we're not going off into the expert report of Petar Vuga and all these military concepts, then I would not file anything." Then we see at the next paragraph: "As a fluent B/C/S and English speaker and professor of managing and command at the Military Academy in Belgrade, the witness will define the most appropriate English words that most clearly reflect the above-mentioned four concepts from Vuga's report."
