Now, it's my understanding we have one concept, "rukovodjenje," that is in dispute. I'm not aware of any other things that are in dispute. I think "rukovodjenje" is -- I have no objection to this witness dealing with "rukovodjenje" in particular, as to translations. Now, we've been asking for a report to try to confirm whether or not this was truly what was in mind. We received a report in Serbian on Wednesday night. We have gone over that report with our interpreters, and I was shocked to find several references in that report to the authorities and responsibilities of the security officer, which is, of course, Mr. Vuga's report. This is the first time we hear that this witness who is a general, who has a very impressive background from what I've seen, is now going to talk about, at the Nth hour, one of the issues of the case which actually has an effect on the commanders of the case, because they tend to -- the security officers in these situations tend to point to the commander and his responsibilities. So when I saw that, I again spoke to my colleague and said, "What is this?" And he said, "Ah, he was just using that as an example of these terms." So I strongly object to this report coming in, in Serbian, on a Wednesday, that it's now getting into issues of import in this case, that I don't have an English copy of, that could open up the cross-examination, the redirect examination, to all these issues that are really meant for Mr. Vuga. I don't object to this witness talking about the translation of "rukovodjenje," that he feels the term would appropriately be "management." We spoke to him briefly. His English is fair. We agree with him that the term "control" in English, as it's used in NATO terminology, incorporates "management," and is not a term such as "passport control," or the limited the way in English also. So I don't think we fundamentally have a very big issue with this witness or what he is saying, but what I don't want is for this to amorph into a discussion of major military concepts, and spend the whole rest of the day in an area that this witness was never designed to talk about. So my request to you would be that this witness be limited to the area of the translation issue, on what word he thinks is appropriate for "rukovodjenje" in English. And if he needs to talk about it in some context to help us put it in context, I have no objection to that. But I don't think anyone should be allowed to take him off into other areas of military expertise in a situation where we have not been forewarned, and there is an expert that's going to be here probably the following week that will deal with that. So let's save some time, deal with this specifically, and get this over with today. I don't see any reason why we can't get this done today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd just like to remind my colleague that we filed our summaries regarding this expert witness, and we said that the expert will explain the main differences between four B/C/S military concepts, not just the terms, "rukovodjenje," "komandovanje," "rukovodjenje u strucnom pogledu," and "kontrola," from the report of Petar Vuga, who disputes between the Defence and the Prosecution arises when we filed the notice and objections to translation of our military expert report. And we have it in our motions and in response to the Prosecution, in our replies, et cetera, and when the Prosecution asked to change the translation into exhibits. So it is our position that this expert should clarify not only the words and the meaning of the words, but to put it in military -- in a military context, to explain the differences between these four military concepts, "rukovodjenje," "kontrola," "rukovodjenje u strucnom pogledu," and "komandovanje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear the translation, as translated by CLSS, for those words, because it was not translated. Can you read it again, and then I would like the interpreters to translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Control, command, "control" in the professional respect, and checking or monitoring.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is now the interpreter's interpretation, not the official CLSS translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to inform the Trial Chamber in the course of the testimony of this witness, we might have some objections to translation of his testimony. And I'll not put these objections immediately in the transcript, but after I view the transcript, the whole of the transcript, and I'll make these objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You all realise that this is very interesting on a Friday afternoon, before lunch, and before the weekend. But what is eating me, actually, my mind, is the following: Isn't Petar Vuga in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't he in a position to explain these words independently of or in respect of, either way, of the way that they have been translated by CLSS? Why do we need another person to deal with the same terms and concepts, when these four words arise out or you can find in Petar Vuga's report, expert report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can hear him after, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, Judge Kwon is making a very good point. Why hear, if at all, Bozidar Forca before Mr. Vuga and not after, if it's necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our idea is that we have a proper translation of Petar Vuga's report; not just his report, but his testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may. There is no controversy here for this witness to testify. We agree with him that "management" is an appropriate English term to be wrapped up into the term "command and control." We agree with him on that. There is no controversy here. There is no reason to call this fine general. I think the proper term here is "dobra danje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you have been saying throughout in the exchange of motions and replies and whatever that we have had the pleasure of reading over the past month and a half. So I think the Prosecution has made its point already on its position as to the concept of rukovodjenje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is "dobra danje."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. That's goodbye, farewell, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Auf Wiedersehen. I suggest that we have -- Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be our preference for this witness to give evidence at some point in time. I think it's only fair for us to say this: The expert that we propose to call and whose report we have served quotes quite extensively from publications of this witness, Mr. Forca, and we were anxious to ask him one or two questions about that. When we saw that his name was on Mr. Zivanovic's list, we rather relied on that and hoped to explore these issues with him. Our time estimate was 30 minutes, and that's how long we think it's going to take. If there's some suggestion that he might return after Mr. Vuga, then we'd certainly support that. I'm bound to say that. We'd endorse, with respect, Judge Kwon's suggestion that that might be the more logical way to proceed if the controversy still persists. But we would be anxious to cross-examine him. That's really all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not closing the doors on anyone, either on the Prosecution or on any one of you. That's not what we meant to say. But I think it's pretty much obvious, or it should be pretty much obvious to everyone, that it appears rather strange, on the face of it, in the first place, that someone is brought before another witness to explain the terms or the significance and the import of the terms and concepts that the other witness, that the subsequent witness is going to use or which are incorporated already in his expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm certainly not going to argue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, what I suggest we do is: We have the break now. We'll give you an opportunity again maybe, Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. McCloskey, to meet and discuss further. In the meantime, we'll have an opportunity to discuss, ourselves, because obviously we haven't seen Mr. Forca's report. We have it, but we don't have it in a language we understand because it hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain it -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would like to make one additional distinction here, and that is that Professor Forca speaks English; whereas, my understanding is that Mr. Vuga does not necessarily speak English as well. So that may explain the order of presentation of these two witnesses. And I would also suggest to you, Mr. President, that once we get into a discussion of the terminologically distinctions between these four words, that necessarily starts to implicate other words. And I think that would have been fairly apparent to the Prosecution some time ago, that once you get into a discussion of terminology of this kind, that necessarily is going to implicate other concepts. Now, certainly, given the practicalities of the timing today, there's no doubt that the Prosecution isn't going to be starting its cross-examination until Monday, and that should give them ample time to prepare for this report and cross-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we still don't have the report, ourselves, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's exactly my point. This implicates that, which implicates that, which implicates all the important military issues of this place. Without a proper report, a proper report in English, this is putting the cart before the horse big time. And there's no reason for it because there is no controversy before us, none. We agree on what is being said, and this is a back-doorway of getting in all this discussion support of this general, and we absolutely object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break -- Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just tell you briefly. Our idea was to bring General Forca to testify just viva voce, without any report, but the Prosecution asked a report at least in B/C/S. And we asked General Forca to make this report in B/C/S, and we provided the Prosecution with this report. And right now, I hear that he has no translation, and he has some objections to such procedure that we provided B/C/S report in written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've heard enough --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, in addition, I would like if Mr. McCloskey could be very clear. If he accepts that the B/C/S word "rukovodjenje u strucnom pogledu" should be translated as "special management" or "managing," and that the word "kontrola" had to be translated as "control," I agree that for the testimony of the witness is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not going to try to replace myself with CLSS. But I have no objection that when we hear these words or when we see them written down, we take into account "management" and we take into account Mr. Vuga's interpretation of what these terms mean. I think that's why I absolutely agree. That's why I say we have no disagreement. CLSS has to pick a word. They can't say two words, and I trust them implicitly on this point. I have no objection to putting those in parentheses on key places and key reports, if that would help. As I say, there's no real difference here, but I don't think we can replace CLSS's interpretation. They have to pick a word. I think they've picked the right word. But the concepts that the general and Vuga talk about, they know about these concepts. We're going to hear their definitions out, and we have no real problems that I know of right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll have the break now, 25 minutes -- half an hour. Yes. We need more time, half an hour, 30 minutes, and then we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, for the record, I notice that Mr. Ostojic is no longer with us. Before the break, we invited you to possibly meet and see if you could find a solution. From the expressions on your faces, I don't think you have even met. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I would recommend the solution that we spoke of in court, and I think perhaps they would agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to add anything to that, Mr. Zivanovic, before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we have discussed and we have come to a conclusion. We are going to tell you what our conclusion is now, in the absence of the witness, but then we will repeat it in his presence so that he understands exactly the parameters within which he needs to limit his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is as follows: First, we have decided that Witness Bozidar Forca will be allowed to testify solely on the discreet linguistic issue identified in the 65 ter summary; that is, the witness will define the most appropriate English words for the concepts mentioned in the 65 ter summary: That is "rukovodjenje," "komandovanje," "rukovodjenje u strucnom pogledu," and "kontrola." He is and will not be heard as a military expert in general. Only the viva voce evidence of the witness will be admitted, which means that his written report, which has already been tendered, will not be admitted and, therefore, will be expunged from the records. We also want to make it clear that in explaining these concepts, the witness may give examples, but he should use general examples and not specific parts of the expert report of Mr. Vuga. Last but not least, Mr. Zivanovic, since this gentleman is your witness, as soon as and after you've introduced yourself to him, we require you to explore his linguistic expertise or proficiency in English, if at all. In other words, you need to start with that first, and then we'll proceed following that. So I think our next step is to bring the witness in. I'll explain to him the parameters of his testimony, as limited by us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Forca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I am very pleased to welcome you to this Tribunal. You've been summoned as an expert witness by the Popovic Defence team. And before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, which is in some domestic jurisdictions equivalent to an oath, to the effect that you'll be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take a seat, make yourself comfortable. Now, welcome once more. You would have gathered, in the few seconds that you were in the courtroom earlier on, that there were some preliminary problems relating to your expected expert testimony. We have been discussing, and we have come to a decision which basically delineates parameters regulating your testimony which are different to those that might have been explained to you when you were engaged by the Popovic Defence team and, more recently, when you were asked to draw up a short expert report. May I just tell you straight away that we have decided that we don't need your written expert report, and that your testimony will, therefore, remain simple viva voce testimony of an expert witness. I know, because we have been told, that in preparing for your testimony, you also had in mind specific parts of the expert report of Mr. Vuga. For the purpose of your testimony today, we have decided that you need to forget all about those excerpts from Mr. Vuga's report; and in your testimony, you are not to refer to Mr. Vuga's report, in whole or in part, at any time. Your testimony will, therefore, be limited to the discreet linguistic issues that have been identified by Mr. Zivanovic, lead counsel for Colonel Popovic, in his 65 ter summary. We are talking of four different terms or concepts. You will pardon my pronunciation of these words in Serbian: One is "rukovodjenje." The other one is "komandovanje." The other one is "rukovodjenje u strucnom pogledu." And the last one is "kontrola." In your testimony, you will need to restrict yourself to defining to us, to the best of your ability, the appropriate corresponding English word for these concepts. You are not being heard and you must not consider yourself here today as a military expert in general. Now, in your explanation to us of the definition of these four concepts, for these four terms, you are, of course, allowed to give examples, but these examples must be general examples; and in giving examples, in other words, you must not refer to any specific part of the expert report of Mr. Vuga. Now, I know, because we have been informed, that you are conversant with both the Serbian language and the English language. If you have any confusion in your mind as to what I have tried to explain to you in simple English terms, please speak out now, after which we then can proceed with your testimony. Have I made myself clear to you? Have I explained the limits that we are more or less establishing regulating your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whatever you said to me is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm happy to hear that, and Mr. Zivanovic will now be putting some questions to you. Please, Mr. Zivanovic, remember to deal with the first issue that we have indicated to you first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Forca. I will not begin with the usual questions that relate to your biography and background; rather, I would start with the question that this Chamber is interested in, and that is your command of the English language. Can you tell us something about that? How well do you speak English, in general? Have you been using it in your practice before, and are you still using it in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I studied English first at the Military Academy course in the years 2001 and 2002. That is called the School for Foreign Languages, which is attended by officers and civilians employed in the army, for their professional purposes. This course lasted ten months. During the course, in 2002, more precisely in April of that year, I was sent to York, England, to St. John College, to attend a three-month course. I studied English there as well. I wasn't aware that I should have brought a certificate with me here. I have a Stanac [phoen] certificate 3232. I would like to note that when using the English language in my work as a teacher, we have very good connoisseurs of English and very good teachers of English in our professional area without relying only what we know and how well we speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he could tell us what this Stanac certificate 3232 is and who issues it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a certificate issued by St. John College, based in York, and it includes four disciplines; listening, writing, understanding, and conversation. All the attendants of the course have to pass these four criteria. According to their criteria, which are actually NATO criteria, the persons who want to work in NATO staff, they need to have the grade of four 3s and above. This is NATO Standard 6001 when we are talking about linguistic faculties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Zivanovic. I'm sorry for that interruption. I don't know whether the witness has answered that part of your question, earlier question, as to whether, since he started his studies in the English language, he's had an opportunity to make use of it in his day-to-day or his ordinary work. I don't recall having heard him answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my next question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Forca, tell me, please, in your everyday work, how much do you use the English language? Do you communicate with your counterparts from other armies, and what is the nature of these contacts?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, ever since I completed the English course in York, that is, in 2002, within my responsibilities, relating primarily to the transformation of military and also the issues that we are discussing today, I attended courses or went on professional visits to English-speaking armed forces. In that respect, I visited the US twice, I went to England, and the school in Germany, to Spain, the NATO Command in Naples, to Norway, and the recently-joined countries of NATO, Slovenia and Bulgaria. I have organised and took part myself in the seminars arranged by representatives of NATO in Serbia, and those were people from Greece, Norway, England, Denmark. In my everyday work, first of all, as a teacher - because I'm the head of the administration of the General Staff, but I also teach in the School for National Defence, and I teach strategy - I use documents written in English; first of all, NATO documents, and specifically individual NATO members' documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, I will now ask you to tell me, or you should better tell us this for the record - I don't know if I asked you this - to give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: My name is Bozidar Forca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of January, 1957, in Serbia, in the village of Obrovac, Backa Palanka municipality, which is in the northern part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: After elementary school and secondary school, I completed Military Academy in Belgrade in 1979. In addition to the Military Academy, I upgraded my professional and scientific knowledge by completing my thesis for an MA, which I did in 1994. In 1997, I finished the School for National Defence, which is the highest level of education that can be acquired within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia. In 2003, I submitted a Ph.D. thesis. In addition to that, as I already mentioned, I attended various courses both at home and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, briefly, something about your career, what you did so far and what posts you held?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: My first duty and my first post, in 1979 until 1991, was in the Military Education Centre of the Army of the JNA in Croatia. To all intents and purposes, I actually discharged two duties at the centre. Initially, I was a commander of the students of the Military Technical Academy, and I remained there until 1985. In that year, I was sent to attend a course for commanders, which was held in Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the commanders of infantry battalions. The course lasted six months. After that, I was transferred to the Department of Military Subjects within the Military Technical Academy. Until 12th December 1991, I taught subjects such as tactics and command and control. I was in Croatia when the combat operation started in 1991, and we were practically under blockade. After negotiations, we were moved to Belgrade. From 1992 onwards, until the year 2002, I worked at the Institute of the Art of War. This institute has been renamed and is now called The Institute for Strategic Research. I worked as a researcher and was the head of the Department for Strategy. At the same time, I also discharged the duties of deputy director of the institute. In 2000, I was transferred to the staff of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, where I stayed for two years. I was deputy head of office. I already said that, in 2002, I went to England to attend a course in the English language. And after completing this course, I was transferred to the School for National Defence, where I was the deputy head of the Department for Strategy. I remained in this post until mid-2005. Since July 2005, I have been working in the administration that I still work at. At the time, it was called Development Administration of the General Staff of the SCG Army, which is Serbian and Montenegrin Army. And in line with NATO designations, I had "G5." First of all, I was the head of the Department for Doctrines within this administration. After that, I became the deputy head of the administration. And in December 2006, I was assigned to my present post, which is the head of the Administration for Planning and Development, and that is designation "J5" of the Army of Serbia. I was promoted in to the rank general last year, "J5."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat which rank were you given last year?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One question more about this: Have you ever been in this Tribunal? Have you appeared here in any capacity whatsoever before?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I appeared before this Tribunal as a military expert in the Prosecution versus Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin case, and I was on the Defence team of Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Forca, what we expect from you today is to provide for us these four definitions that you have been advised earlier. But before that, can you tell us what, in the Serbian language, these terms mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the notions and terms, and they are linguistic expressions, are extremely important. If you take a general aspect that people can communicate and understand each other, and if you look at it from a professional angle, they are extremely important for an exact and accurate establishment of scientific, social, or other spheres in which human beings are involved. In that sense, according to the theory of logics, in our science, a notion is defined as a perception of an object that we have in mind; not the object itself, but our meditative perception of this object. Speaking of these four particular terms, it is very important that we distinguish the scope of the notion, on the one hand, and the substance of the notion, on the other. The substance particularly implies this perception of an object that can be part of physical or mental reality. For example, I am sitting here on this chair. My perception of the chair is not that it is composed of four legs and other parts, but, rather, that this is part of furniture the purpose of which is for sitting. When determining the substance, it is the basic rule of defining always implies, which in Latin is "genus proximum specifica diferencia," which means we link a certain notion to a higher gender and then we specify the differences between this one and other notions on this level. I have taken the example of the notion of a chair, linked it to a higher level of furniture, and on this higher level of furniture you have beds, you have tables, you have cupboards, et cetera. A chair differs from these other items is that it is used for sitting. One cannot sit on a table. On the other hand, the scope of a notion implies, and this is going to be very important when we come to the comparison between command and control, the scope of a notion implies all lower-ranging notions of generality to which this specific notion refers. For example, if we say this notion, the former JNA, the extent of or the expanse of this army includes branches, combat arms, and services; then it can be further fragmented into commands, units, and installations; then you can fragment units further on into corps, brigade, battalions, companies, squads, et cetera. All of these elements are incorporated in the notion of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which methodology is applied in the military theory, or, rather, how does one arrive at a term which signifies a certain notion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: As I've already said, a word or a term is the linguistic expression of a notion. Now, how does one arrive at such a word? Well, under our theory of the Serbian language and the military theory, you can arrive there in two ways: First, in a scientifically-determined way. We are aware of the fact that not only in the Serbian language, but in other languages as well, there exists the following problem, in scientifically-defining a given word. For that reason, in trying to find the linguistic expressions or terms of a notion, one resorts to conventions, which can have the global, worldwide character. I will give you an illustration. I will not be clarifying the example any further. But in the UN in 1974, "aggression" was defined. Now, how was this done, and what did the term of "aggression" imply? The United Nations adopted Resolution 1133 following numerous discussions. Even at this global level, there is a difficulty in defining a given term. In order to arrive at a term for a given notion in the military science, we have been using, and we are still using three methods: First, if a word exists in the standard usage or vernacular, then the term, the word that exists is used, such as, for instance, "soldier." Second, through our adopting foreign words, either directly or by adapting them to the Serbian language. Third, directly adopting, literally adopting, a foreign word. For instance, in the Serbian language, the term "dvopek" is used, which is -- or, rather, the word "doppler" is used, which is directly taken from the German language. That is why word formation is not a problem that is experienced only by us, and it is an area that has not been developed enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be moving on to an issue that is more specifically of interest to us. In the theory and practice of the Yugoslav People's Army, which is the subject of our interest, what was the way in which the term "command and control" was used, "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, when it comes to these two terms, what comes into mind is the legislation; namely, laws, regulations and doctrinary documents such as rules and instructions which were used by the then-JNA. An analysis of these documents - and I know that the ICTY has all these documents, i.e., Law on the All People's Defence, the rules governing corps, the rules governing battalions, companies, and squads - will indicate that these complex terms were used: "Rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," that is, command and control as a single expression; and that "komandovanje," "command," was used on its own as well, which is something which appears in the rules governing brigades, companies, and squads. Most of the documents used by the then-JNA used this compound expression, "command and control," "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To pick up from what you've just said, in what way did the JNA form and use these expressions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In answering this question, I will refer to Professor Dr. Branislav Jovanovic, who was one of the leading individuals when it came to the Yugoslav Army's theory. He wrote a document in 1984 which was called "An Introduction into the Control-and-Command Theory." Looking at the genesis and the relationship between the two terms, he established that the notions of control and command, "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," were used interchangeably as synonyms. That was one aspect of it. The other aspect of it was these were two function of the same substance, so that somebody -- while one person would use "rukovodjenje," the other would use "komandovanje." And the third aspect, which he personally agreed with, was that "komandovanje" was a function or a part of "rukovodjenje." If I go back to the legislation and doctrinary documents that I've mentioned, and if we tie this up with what I've just said about the scope or the extent of a given term, we will establish the following: The instructions for the commands and staffs, the rules governing corps, the rules governing battalions, all of them use the syntax as a compound expression; namely, "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje." The instruction for the work of command staffs and the rules governing corps, as terms that are at the lower level of generality and define control and command, we had "planiranje," "plan"; "organizovanje," "organising"; "koordinacija," "coordinating"; and "kontrola," which in methodological term is incorrect, that a term which is not as general, for instance, "komandovanje," should appear as a heading in describing something at a lower level. If we look at the rules governing battalions, which also use the compound expression "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," and if we look at the rules governing brigades, which only use the term "komandovanje," we will see that the scope of the two notions is, in fact, the same and comprises the lower-level functions of "planiranje"; "organizovanje"; "naredjivanje," in other words, "ordering"; and "kontrola." In that sense, if two different notions have the same scope, then they become synonyms, they are synonyms, which is the case in the case of "komandovanje," which was improperly used by the rules governing brigades. In 1982, having realised this problem, a group of military experts tried to distinguish between the notions of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," and produced a document entitled "Certain Issues Concerning Command and Control," "Rukovodjenje and Komandovanje," are within the forces of SFRY. That document was marked as "strictly confidential" at the time. I will not be reading or quoting what the author's military experts wrote about this. They, under the notion of "rukovodjenje," included primarily the aspect of social monitoring, and I'm speaking about the armed forces: Organisation, development, procurement for and organisation, as well as other activities which related to the armed forces. I will be using an English expression for the first time. This could be interpreted as "management," it could be translated as "management." On the other hand, the notion of "komandovanje" was accepted as being used on its own with regard to the three main duties and obligations of an individual; namely, to take a decision, to issue an order in accordance with a decision made, and to control or monitor or follow up on what he has ordered. This distinction had the following bearing on the regulations of the JNA, and that was that the subsequent JNA regulations mostly used the compound expression of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your research as an expert on the issue of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," what is your personal position with regard to these notions, to these terms?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said at the outset, when I look at the relationship between these two notions, I have to start and proceed from the Serbian language from which certain terms were and were not used. This is one aspect of the definition of a notion. In our language, the terms "upravljati" and "rukovoditi" are synonymous. "Rukovodjenje" is seen as "upravlanje" in -- it is more specifically defined as "upravlanje," "managing." "Komandovanje" is not a term that existed in our language. It was a term taken from a foreign language. Words that are associated in the Serbian language, and which would correspond to "komandovanje," are "narediti," "order"; or "naredjivati" as "ordering"; "zapovedati" or "zapovediti," which is the same. At the time, we had Serbo-Croat, so "naredjivati" would be more from the Serbian language and "zapovediti" from the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both mean "order," "to order."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: So it is not on this basis that we can establish that "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje" are synonymous. The terms "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," as far as their meaning goes, as their substance, they can be defined as a process by which individual commands and units of the JNA are guided in implementing their tasks with a view to achieving their planned objective or goal. That would be the substance of the notion of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje." Now, the scope of the notion of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje" would envelope the process functions: "Planning," "planiranje," or "organising," "organizovanje"; and "ordering," "naredjivanje"; "coordination," "koordinacija"; and "kontrola." Now, the process of "rukovodjenje" has to be seen from two other angles: One is the process of the work of a Command; and the other the relationship between the process functions, the one that I've mentioned a moment ago, and the so-called departmental functions or activities carried out by a Command. If we look at the process of the work of a Command, it has its customary activities. I will enumerate them now. I don't have the opportunity of making a diagram of them, but I can enumerate them. Once an assignment is received, the following activities ensue at the Command: Studying the assignment, issuing preliminary orders, drafting the plan of work of the Command, the Command's familiarising with the assignment, the basic idea of the commander, conveying the basic idea, situation assessment, submitting of proposals, decision-making, drafting of the plans or documents of a given combat activity, and conveying the information to the subordinates, and, lastly, "kontrola." This is the full process which can be shortened for various reasons. Within this process, the notion of "komandovanje" appears. When the decision has to be taken, when it has to be conveyed to the subordinates, and when it has to be monitored or "kontrolisati." So the process includes the issuing of the order, which is then followed up on the B/C/S term "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they control, "kontrola," what do they control?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The commander controls whether the order issued was implemented or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The command organs, within the process that I've just described, have just one commander. We have one commander; whereas, we have the command organs which do "rukovodjenje," which means that they take part in planning, proposing, coordinating, and implementing the commander's order. The other aspect of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje" is the relationship between these process functions, which include planning, organising, and all the way down to "kontrola," and these departmental tasks. All the documents of the units state that the composition of a given unit and the use it will be put to will depend on what the varied composition of the unit is and on the activities discharged by the Command. Depending on the tasks that the Command has to carry out, adequate services, professional services are organised at the Command. If we look at a corps of the land forces, the professional organs of the Command include the staff, logistics organ, organ for the cooperation with socio-political organisations, organ for development and financing, and security organ. They were set up for the purposes of the Command's activities, and these activities can be of those of the Command staff, security, of logistics, political, or legal activities. So what does the "rukovodjenje" of a Command mean? Any activity which falls within these various departments overlaps with the various processes. For instance, the logistic support must be planned, organised, orders must be issued, there must be coordination, and there must be control of its implementation. That is this other relationship within the command-and-control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you've just said about command and control, what would you say is the definition of "strucno rukovodjenje" and "kontrola"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, you'll allow me to start from the latter notion of "kontrola." In the Serbian language, this is a notion or a term which was not contested in any other document in the context of command and control. In all the documents, "kontrola" is one of the functions of command and control. As the instructions for the work of commands and staffs reads, "kontrola" means the process function of "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," which establishes the distinction between the values that were planned and the values that were achieved in the process of "kontrola." Therefore, "kontrola" allows to -- one to have an insight into the degree to which certain orders were carried out or certain assignments were carried out by the commands, staffs, units, and individuals. "Kontrola" was performed by commanding officers, both commanders and "komandiri," and special -- specially-organised organs of command and control. The method and type of "kontrola" was determined by the commanding officer of a unit. The other notion of "strucno rukovodjenje" does not exist as such in our dictionaries. It was a coined expression. In order to answer the question of what this notion stands for, what we believe it stands for, it is necessary to describe the relations that were valid at the time within control and command, and that are still valid and a part of the command of every unit. In this sense, Your Honours, there existed three types of relations. The first type was the command or line relationship, which was established on the superior/subordinate line; for instance, brigade commander/battalion commander, battalion commander/company commander. The other relationship of the command-and-control relationship is the staff relationship. "Staff relationship" stands for a special method of work of the Command which drafts proposals and submits proposals to the commander in the decision-making process. This relationship existed only on one level, regardless of the unit. Suffice it, that a unit had its command, whether it is a company, battalion, brigade, or a corps. In other words, the commander of that unit of the corps, brigade, or battalion had this line relationship toward his assistants and the chief of staff, and they had this staff relationship vis a vis the commander. There was a third type of a relationship or relationships which were functional relationships, such as, for instance, logistics support, engineers' support, and such like. So these were called "functions." Every Command had an expert or professional organ for these functions. This organ was in a functional relationship with its counterpart at a lower level. For instance, the brigade logistics organ was in a functional relationship with the assistant commander for logistics of a battalion, and in a functional relationship with the unit providing logistics support. A chief of artillery who is, let's say, a member of a staff stands in a functional relationship toward a commander of an artillery unit of a brigade, for instance, because the principle of the singleness of command was in place. Allow me to conclude this topic of these various relationships. This means that "strucno rukovodjenje" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The objections is just that this is getting a long way from what's needed to explain and define the terminology and seems to be explaining the structure of the forces, and in relation to the structure that we're objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zivanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the other microphone off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is not the structure of forces, but just an illustration of this a little bit abstract theory, military theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue and finish, please. Yes, General, the last few questions before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you conclude what you were saying, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the notion of "strucno rukovodjenje" did not exist as a specific term, there was "rukovodjenje u strucnom smislu," which means this notion can be regarded in the following light: The professional or expert organs, the "rukovode," what do they do? They engage in "rukovodjenje" of the function that they were given responsibility for, as an expert or professional organ, and they engage in "rukovodjenje" in the professional sense of their subordinate professional organs. "Strucno rukovodjenje" is a narrower term compared to "rukovodjenje" in general, which applies to the entire unit and assignment. So it's a -- it's a narrower term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid we have to leave it at that for today. General, we'll see you again on Monday morning. Have a good rest. It's a very complicated subject, yours, and we'll use the weekend to ruminate and inwardly digest the depth of what you've been saying. So we stand adjourned until Monday morning at 9.00. Thank you.
